title: Go Slices & Maps: The Field Manual
summary: A deep tour of Go's two workhorse data structures — how slices sit on backing arrays and grow through append, and how maps hash, iterate, and mutate — with the aliasing, growth, and iteration bugs that bite in real code.

chapters.title: Arrays vs Slices: The Foundation
points: An array `[5]int` has its length baked into its type: `[5]int` and `[6]int` are different types and cannot be assigned to each other
Arrays are values: assigning or passing an array copies every element
`len()` of an array is a compile-time constant; the compiler can fold it
A slice is NOT an array — it is a 3-word struct: `{ptr *T, len int, cap int}` (24 bytes on 64-bit)
The slice header is a value; copying a slice copies 3 words, not the elements
The `ptr` field points into a backing array that lives elsewhere (heap or stack)
`len` = how many elements you may index; `cap` = how many exist from `ptr` to the end of the backing array
Indexing beyond `len` panics: `runtime error: index out of range [5] with length 3`, even if `cap` is larger
Slice literal `[]int{1,2,3}` allocates a backing array of 3 and points at it
Array literal `[3]int{1,2,3}` IS the data; `[...]int{1,2,3}` lets the compiler count
The zero value of a slice is `nil`: `ptr=nil, len=0, cap=0` — safe to `append` to, safe to `range` over, safe to `len()`
`var s []int` (nil) vs `s := []int{}` (non-nil, len 0): both len 0, but `s == nil` differs, and `encoding/json` marshals them as `null` vs `[]`
Slices are not comparable: `s1 == s2` is a compile error; only `s == nil` is allowed
Rule of thumb: use arrays for fixed-size value semantics (hash digests, coordinates), slices for everything else

chapters.title: The Backing Array & Slice Expressions
points: `s[low:high]` yields `len = high-low`, `cap = cap(s)-low`, and shares the SAME backing array
Slicing never copies element data — it only builds a new 3-word header
Defaults: `s[:3]` means `s[0:3]`, `s[2:]` means `s[2:len(s)]`, `s[:]` is the whole slice
Slicing an array takes its address: `a := [5]int{}; s := a[1:3]` — `s` points into `a`, so writes through `s` change `a`
You may slice up to `cap`, not just `len`: `s[:cap(s)]` legally re-exposes elements past `len`
Re-slicing past `len` resurrects stale data — elements you thought were dropped are still readable
Three-index slice `s[low:high:max]` sets `cap = max-low`, clamping how far append may reach
Full slice expression is the standard defensive tool: `s[i:j:j]` gives `cap == len`, forcing the next append to copy
The backing array stays alive as long as ANY slice points at it — a 3-byte slice of a 10 MB read pins all 10 MB
Fix for the pin: copy out what you need — `out := make([]byte, len(part)); copy(out, part)` — or `bytes.Clone(part)`
`copy(dst, src)` copies `min(len(dst), len(src))` elements and returns that count; it never grows `dst`
`copy` handles overlapping slices correctly (memmove semantics), so `copy(s[1:], s[:len(s)-1])` shifts right safely
Delete in place, order-preserving: `s = append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...)`
Delete fast, order-destroying: `s[i] = s[len(s)-1]; s = s[:len(s)-1]`
After deleting pointer elements, nil the tail slot (`s[len(s)-1] = nil`) or the removed pointer leaks

chapters.title: append and Growth Mechanics
points: `append` returns a new slice header — you MUST use the return value; `append(s, x)` alone is a wasted call (vet flags it)
If `len < cap`, append writes into the existing backing array in place and returns a header with `len+1`
If `len == cap`, append allocates a NEW bigger array, copies the old elements, and returns a header pointing to the new array
That reallocation is exactly why aliases silently split apart — see the aliasing chapter
Growth is amortized: doubling gives O(1) amortized cost per append, O(n) worst case for a single call
Go 1.18+ growth rule: below the 256-element threshold, cap roughly doubles; above it, it grows by ~1.25x plus a smoothing term, then is rounded up to a size class
Because of size-class rounding, the resulting cap is often larger than the formula predicts — never hardcode expected cap values in tests
`append(s, other...)` appends a whole slice; `append(b, "str"...)` is the special case for appending a string to `[]byte`
Growing once beats growing many times: `make([]T, 0, n)` when `n` is known removes all intermediate copies and garbage
`make([]T, n)` gives len n of zero values — `append` on it adds AFTER those zeros, a classic off-by-n bug
Appending to a `nil` slice is legal and idiomatic: `var s []int; s = append(s, 1)` allocates on first use
`slices.Grow(s, n)` reserves room for n more elements without changing `len`
`slices.Clip(s)` returns `s[:len(s):len(s)]`, cutting cap down to len
Complexity table: index O(1), append amortized O(1), prepend O(n), delete-ordered O(n), delete-swap O(1), copy O(n), search O(n)

chapters.title: Aliasing Bugs: When Two Slices Are One
points: Core hazard: whether append mutates a shared array or forks off a private copy depends on spare capacity — a runtime property, not a visible one
The classic: `a := []int{1,2,3,4,5}; b := a[:2]; b = append(b, 99)` — `a[2]` is now 99, because `b` had spare cap
Same code with `b := a[:2:2]` leaves `a` untouched: append is forced to allocate
So a bug can appear or vanish based on capacity the caller never sees — the worst kind of nondeterminism
Function taking `[]T` can mutate the caller's elements: passing a slice does not protect the data, only the header
A function CANNOT change the caller's `len` — the header is a copy — so callee-side `append` results must be returned
Two slices from the same array can partially overlap, making `copy` behave in surprising but well-defined ways
`append(x, y...)` where x and y share an array is safe (append copies before overwriting), but hand-rolled loops in that shape are not
Returning `s[i:j]` from a parser hands the caller a window into a buffer you plan to reuse — the classic reuse-corruption bug
`bufio.Scanner.Bytes()` is exactly that: the returned slice is invalidated by the next `Scan()`; use `Text()` or clone it
Struct fields holding slices are shallow-copied on struct assignment — the two structs share the same elements
Defensive copy pattern for constructors and getters: clone the input slice before storing, clone the field before returning
`slices.Clone(s)` is the idiomatic one-liner; note it is still a SHALLOW copy — inner slices and pointers stay shared
Detection tips: reproduce with `-race` if goroutines are involved, and print `len`/`cap` at the suspicious call to see the fork point

chapters.title: Slices in Practice: Ranging, Passing, Pooling
points: `for i, v := range s` copies each element into `v`; writing to `v` changes nothing in `s`
Mutate via index instead: `for i := range s { s[i] *= 2 }`
Ranging a big-struct slice copies each struct — use `for i := range s` and `&s[i]` when the element is fat
`range` evaluates the slice expression once: `len` is captured at loop start, so appending inside the loop does not extend the iteration
But appending inside a range loop CAN reallocate, so `&s[i]` taken earlier may point at the dead old array
Go 1.22+ gives each iteration a fresh `i` and `v`, so capturing them in a closure or goroutine is now safe — pre-1.22 code needed `v := v`
Go 1.22+ also allows `for i := range n` over an integer, replacing the classic three-clause count loop
Passing a slice is cheap (24 bytes) — do not add a `*[]T` parameter just for performance
Use `*[]T` only when the callee must change the caller's length or replace the slice wholesale
Accept `[]T` in parameters, but return concrete slices; accepting the widest useful type is a caller kindness
Reuse the buffer between iterations with `buf = buf[:0]` — keeps the capacity, resets the length, zero allocations
`sync.Pool` of slices amplifies aliasing risk: whatever you handed out must not be retained after `Put`
Preallocation with a known length: `out := make([]T, 0, len(in))` before a map/filter loop
`clear(s)` (Go 1.21+) zeroes all elements of a slice without changing len or cap
Prefer `slices` package helpers: `Contains`, `Index`, `Sort`, `SortFunc`, `BinarySearch`, `Equal`, `Reverse`, `Compact`, `Insert`, `Delete`

chapters.title: Maps: Structure and Basic Mechanics
points: `map[K]V` is a hash table; the map variable is a pointer to the runtime hmap struct, so maps are reference-like
The zero value of a map is `nil`: reads and `len` work and return zero values, but ANY write panics with `assignment to entry in nil map`
Always construct before writing: `m := make(map[string]int)` or `m := map[string]int{}`
`make(map[K]V, hint)` presizes for roughly `hint` entries, avoiding repeated growth and rehashing
Reading a missing key returns the zero value of V, never an error — `m["nope"]` on `map[string]int` gives 0
The comma-ok form distinguishes absent from zero: `v, ok := m[k]`
`delete(m, k)` is a no-op if the key is absent and never panics; `delete` on a nil map is also safe
`len(m)` is O(1); there is no `cap()` for maps
Key type must be comparable: no slices, maps, or functions as keys — the compiler rejects them
Structs and arrays ARE valid keys if all their fields are comparable — handy for composite keys
Interface keys compile but panic at runtime if the dynamic type is not comparable
NaN as a float key is pathological: `NaN != NaN`, so each insert makes a new unreachable entry
Values are not addressable: `m[k].field = v` is a compile error for struct values — read out, modify, write back, or store `map[K]*V`
Set idiom: `map[string]struct{}` uses zero bytes per value; `map[string]bool` is more readable — pick one and stay consistent
Maps are not comparable: use `maps.Equal(m1, m2)` (Go 1.21+) instead of `==`
Complexity: average O(1) lookup, insert, delete; growth is amortized, with individual writes occasionally paying for incremental rehash work

chapters.title: Map Internals: Buckets, Growth, Swiss Tables
points: Classic Go map layout: an array of buckets, each holding up to 8 key/value pairs
The low-order hash bits select the bucket; the high 8 bits are cached as `tophash` for fast in-bucket rejection
Keys and values are stored in separate arrays inside the bucket, avoiding padding between differently sized types
When a bucket fills past 8, an overflow bucket is chained onto it — long chains degrade lookups toward O(n)
Load factor 6.5 per bucket triggers growth: buckets double and entries are rehashed
Growth is INCREMENTAL — each write evacuates a bucket or two, so no single operation stalls on a full rehash
During evacuation the map holds both `buckets` and `oldbuckets`; reads must check both
Same-size growth exists too: when a map is mostly tombstones from deletes, it rehashes into equally many buckets to compact
Go 1.24 replaced this with Swiss tables: groups of 8 slots plus an SIMD-scannable control word of 7-bit hash fragments
Swiss tables measurably cut lookup time and memory for large maps and changed the internal layout, but the language semantics are unchanged
Map hashing is randomly seeded per process to defeat hash-flooding denial of service — a direct cause of unordered iteration
Maps never shrink their bucket count on delete: a map that once held 1M entries keeps that memory even at `len(m) == 0`
To actually reclaim it, build a fresh map and drop the old one; `clear(m)` empties entries but keeps the buckets
Large keys or values are stored indirectly (pointer to heap) above a size threshold, so consider `map[K]*BigStruct` deliberately rather than by accident
You cannot take the address of a map element because growth relocates entries — that is the root reason for the non-addressability rule

chapters.title: Map Iteration Order & Deleting During Range
points: Map iteration order is deliberately randomized — the runtime picks a random start bucket AND a random offset within the bucket
This is a feature, not an accident: it stops code from depending on an order the implementation is free to change
So two ranges over the SAME unmodified map in the same program can yield different orders
Never build a test that asserts map range order — it will pass locally and fail in CI
For deterministic output, collect keys and sort: `keys := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))` (Go 1.23+), then range the keys
`fmt` prints maps in sorted key order, which lulls people into thinking iteration is ordered — it is not
Deleting during range is explicitly safe: entries deleted before being reached will NOT be produced
Deleting the CURRENT key while ranging is the standard filter idiom and is fully defined behavior
Adding during range is unspecified: a new entry may or may not be visited in that same loop
Worst case, add-during-range makes a nonterminating loop, so build a second map or collect keys first instead
Concurrent map access is a different problem entirely: the runtime aborts with `fatal error: concurrent map writes` — a crash you cannot recover
That fatal error is a best-effort detector, not a guarantee; use `-race` to catch it reliably
Concurrent read-only access is safe with no synchronization, as long as no goroutine is writing
Guard with `sync.RWMutex` for general use, or `sync.Map` for the specific shapes it targets: append-only caches and disjoint key sets per goroutine
`maps.Keys` / `maps.Values` (Go 1.23+) return iterators — pair with `slices.Collect` or `slices.Sorted` to materialize

chapters.title: Slice vs Map: Choosing and Trading Off
points: Slice: ordered, index-addressable, contiguous, cache-friendly, O(n) search
Map: unordered, key-addressable, scattered, pointer-chasing, O(1) average lookup
Crossover reality: for small n (roughly under 8-16 elements), a linear scan of a slice often BEATS a map lookup because of cache locality and hashing cost
Memory: a slice pays `cap * sizeof(T)`; a map pays buckets, tophashes, and up to ~2x slack from load factor and growth
Iteration: slices iterate in order at memory speed; maps iterate randomly with a bucket walk
Insertion at end: slice amortized O(1), map O(1) — but the slice does not need to hash
Insertion in middle: slice O(n) shift, map has no concept of position
Deletion: slice O(n) ordered or O(1) swap-remove, map O(1) with no reordering
Duplicates: slices allow them, maps collapse them by key — the fastest dedupe is `map[T]struct{}` plus an output slice for order
Determinism: slices give stable order for free; maps require an explicit sort step
Serialization: JSON arrays preserve order; JSON objects from Go maps are emitted with sorted keys by `encoding/json`
Zero value: `nil` slice is fully usable for append; `nil` map is read-only and panics on write — a key asymmetry to memorize
Common hybrid: a slice for order plus a `map[K]int` index into it — an ordered map, at the cost of keeping both in sync on delete
Decision rule: need order or small n, use a slice; need keyed lookup at scale, use a map; need both, keep both and encapsulate them behind a type

chapters.title: Top Mistakes & Field-Tested Rules
points: Ignoring append's return value — the mutation may go nowhere; `go vet` catches this one
`make([]T, n)` when you meant `make([]T, 0, n)` — you get n zeros followed by your data
Writing to a nil map — build it in the constructor, not lazily at the call site
Assuming map range order is stable, especially in tests and golden-file output
Reading a missing key and treating the zero value as real data — use comma-ok when absence is meaningful
Returning a sub-slice of a reusable buffer, so the caller's data mutates under them later
Holding a small slice of a huge read and pinning the whole backing array in memory
Taking `&s[i]` and then appending, leaving the pointer aimed at the abandoned old array
Forgetting `s[i:j:j]` when handing a slice to code that will append to it
Nil-ing removed pointer elements is not optional when the slice outlives the removal — otherwise the objects leak
Trying `m[k].field = x` on a struct-valued map and reaching for reflection instead of `map[K]*V`
Assuming `clear(m)` frees memory — it empties entries, it does not shrink buckets
Concurrent map writes without a lock, which is a fatal crash rather than a recoverable error
Mental model to keep: a slice is a WINDOW onto an array, and append either writes through the window or silently cuts a new one

Checklist before shipping: run `go vet`, run tests with `-race`, presize with `make(..., 0, n)` where n is known, clone at every API boundary that stores or returns a slice, and sort keys anywhere map output is user-visible
